extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (PR managers, consultants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for designing, implementing, and evaluating public relations programs, including formative and summative research, decision rules about when to measure, steps to prepare for evaluation, and detailed evaluation questions for conception, implementation, and impact assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delineate specific targets
rubrics_metrics.description: After middle-range objectives are set, give careful consideration to delineating specific targets in terms of their demographic and psychological attributes, their life-style, value and belief systems, and mass media habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important to determine the scope of prior indifference and to uncover its roots; specific targeting improves the chance that information giving will influence behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hesitation in crisis communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Hesitation — which leads to public perception of confusion, callousness, incompetence, or lack of preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act promptly in crises to avoid negative public perceptions; hesitation undermines trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obfuscation in crisis communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Obfuscation — which leads to the perception of dishonesty and insensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be clear and transparent; obfuscation damages credibility and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid retaliation in crisis communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Retaliation — which increases tension and intensifies emotions rather than reducing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not escalate conflict; retaliation prolongs and intensifies crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prevarication or equivocation in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevarication or equivocation — which creates the biggest problem, because nothing substitutes for truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell the truth; equivocation creates severe credibility problems and hinders resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pontification in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Pontification — which creates vulnerability by taking a high-handed approach without really dealing with the issue at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid moralizing or lecturing; address the substantive issues directly and humbly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confrontation in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Confrontation — which provides others visibility by keeping the issue alive, giving them a platform, and giving them more to respond to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from confrontational tactics that elevate opponents and prolong visibility of the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid litigation as an initial crisis tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation — which guarantees even greater visibility and may eliminate more reasonable solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that immediate legal action can increase visibility and foreclose alternative, reasonable resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design messages for situation, time, place, and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective communication messages must be designed for the situation, time, place, and audience; it requires careful selection of media and technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no surefire universal rules for message development — tailor messages and media to context and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure source/sender credibility and competence
rubrics_metrics.description: The communicator must have adequate information and credibility in the eyes of the receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational performance and demonstrated desire to serve stakeholders build credibility; sender competence on the subject matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use channels that will carry the message to the receiver
rubrics_metrics.description: The communicator must use a channel that will carry the message to the receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select channels that the target publics use and respect; different channels serve different stages of diffusion and have different perceived values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make messages decodable, comprehensible, and relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: The message must be within the receiver’s capacity to decode and comprehend and be relevant to the receiver’s interests or needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider availability, habits, reading ability, prior knowledge; message complexity should decrease the farther it must travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate receiver self-interest to cause a response
rubrics_metrics.description: The message must motivate the receiver’s self-interest and cause a response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective messages connect to what receivers perceive as rewards or benefits and prompt measurable responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility (one of the seven Cs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication starts with a climate of belief. This climate is built by performance on the part of the organization, reflecting an earnest desire to serve stakeholders and publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance drives organizational reputation; receivers must have confidence in the sender and regard the source's competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context (one of the seven Cs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A communications program must square with the realities of its environment. Mass media only supplement the words and deeds of daily living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context must provide for participation and playback; it must confirm, not contradict, the message; effective communication needs a supportive social environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content (one of the seven Cs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The message must have meaning for receivers, and it must be compatible with their value system. It must have relevance to the receivers’ situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People select information promising the greatest rewards; content determines the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (one of the seven Cs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The message must be put in simple terms. Words must mean the same to the receivers as to the sender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex issues should be compressed into themes, slogans, or stereotypes with simplicity and clarity; simpler for longer-distance diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and consistency (one of the seven Cs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication is an unending process. It requires repetition to achieve penetration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition with variation aids learning and persuasion; the story must be consistent and the organization should 'speak with one voice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels (one of the seven Cs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Established channels of communication should be used—channels that receivers use and respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating new channels can be difficult and expensive; selective channels required for target publics; new media can facilitate participation and overcome rhetorical obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capability of the audience (one of the seven Cs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication must take into account the capability of the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications are most effective when they require the least effort from receivers; consider availability, habits, reading ability, and prior knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand communication, media, and audience effects theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must understand communication, media effects theory, and audience effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move beyond simple transmission models; audiences may ignore, reject, misinterpret, and reinterpret messages—understanding these effects is fundamental to evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish outputs from outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the difference between outputs (effort and process) and outcomes (impact and effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbers of releases, clippings, or attendees are outputs, not end points; evaluation should focus on outcomes and program impact, not just activity counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate SMART objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives need to be specific, measurable, achievable, realistic (or relevant), and time bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid broad, imprecise objectives (e.g., 'increase awareness' without benchmarks). Include baseline, target, audience, and timeframe in objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be numeric as well as rhetorical
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should learn basic skills in math and statistics to generate and present data to inform, support, test, manage, and evaluate programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Management expects numeric evidence (ROI, brand value, reputation metrics); poor numerical literacy undermines credibility and budget support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not measure when you cannot make a difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Forget measurement when you cannot make a difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the organization lacks the capacity to change the outcome (e.g., management decisions are final), measurement may be a waste of resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not measure when unwilling to implement changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Forget measurement when you’re unwilling to do what it takes to make things better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement only matters if the organization is prepared to act on findings; otherwise it's futile or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not measure when measurement costs exceed program value
rubrics_metrics.description: Forget measurement when it’s more expensive to measure than the program you’re measuring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh measurement costs against expected value; advanced attribution work can be costly and should be used judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure when you care if it’s working
rubrics_metrics.description: Do measurement when you care about whether what you’re doing is working or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If objectives are SMART, measure to track progress against benchmarks, targets, and timeframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure when you know you need to change
rubrics_metrics.description: Do measurement when you know you need to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use data to drive decisions; measurement supports data-driven changes rather than intuition alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure when you need numbers for stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Do measurement when you need numbers to share with the numbers people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide metrics such as share of voice, tone comparison, message presence, and correlations (e.g., coverage to web traffic) to satisfy management and funders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formative and summative research appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Research before and during implementation to inform planning and adjustment is formative research; research after the program to assess progress and impact is summative research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation research encompasses both and should be used strategically for planning, managing, and evaluating PR programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess extent and distribution of target problem/population
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation should determine what is the extent and distribution of the target problem and/or population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use baseline and benchmark research to understand scope and to design interventions appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess program design conformity with intended goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the program designed in conformity with intended goals; is there a coherent rationale underlying it; and have chances of successful delivery been maximized?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate program logic, rationale, and implementation feasibility before and during rollout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess projected costs relative to benefits and effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: What are projected or existing costs, and what is their relation to benefits and effectiveness?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include cost–benefit considerations in design and post-implementation evaluation (efficiency analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor target reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the program reaching the specified target population or target area?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track distribution and penetration among identified publics; adjust channels and tactics if coverage is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor fidelity of implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the intervention efforts being conducted as specified in the program design?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether activities occur as planned (process evaluation) to distinguish implementation failure from design failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess program effectiveness in achieving intended goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the program effective in achieving its intended goals?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure outcomes against SMART objectives and benchmarks to document impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative explanations for observed results
rubrics_metrics.description: Can the results of the program be explained by some alternative process that does not include the program?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use research designs and controls where possible to attribute causality and isolate program effects from confounders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify unintended effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the program having some effects that were not intended?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for collateral or negative outcomes and incorporate findings into future planning and risk assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate costs to deliver services vs benefits to participants
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the costs to deliver services and benefits to program participants?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include per-participant or per-output cost metrics when assessing program utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess program efficiency vs alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the program an efficient use of resources, compared with alternative uses of the resources?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare cost-effectiveness across possible interventions to inform resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pseudoresearch
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation research should be used to learn what happened and why, not to prove or justify something already done; avoid 'symbolic' evaluation or pseudoresearch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pseudoresearch motives include organizational politics (justify decisions), service promotion (slanted studies), and personal satisfaction (ego-bolstering); such efforts are self-defeating and undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish agreement on uses and purposes of evaluation (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish agreement on the uses and purposes of the evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commit to paper the problem or question motivating research and detail how findings will be used; this avoids unused or useless data and helps specify briefs for outside vendors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure organizational commitment and make research basic to the program (Step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secure organizational commitment to evaluation and make research basic to the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain buy-in and resources; embed evaluation in program planning so research is integral rather than an afterthought.
